title: What is an API Gateway and when does a system need one?
description: The single-entry-point pattern: routing, cross-cutting concerns, BFF variants, and the failure modes gateways concentrate.

data.text: **Question:** What is an API Gateway and when does a system need one?

An API Gateway is the **single entry point** in front of your services that **routes** requests to the right backend, and applies **cross-cutting concerns once**: authentication/token validation, rate limiting, TLS termination, request transformation, caching, observability, and protocol translation (HTTP/gRPC/WebSocket). The **Backend-For-Frontend (BFF)** variant gives each client (web, iOS, Android) its own gateway shaped for its needs — the web app gets aggregates, the mobile gets minimal payloads. You need one when clients face N services directly: without it, every client re-implements auth, versioning, and discovery. The price: it's on the critical path — a **single point of failure and a bottleneck** — so it must be kept thin (no business logic), deployed safely, and scaled deliberately.

**What belongs in the gateway:**
- **Routing/rewriting**: /api/orders → Order service, /api/products → Catalog
- **AuthN at the edge**: validate JWT/session once, forward identity claims — services still do AuthZ for their own resources
- **Rate limiting / quotas**: per-user, per-client; protects downstream services (429 + Retry-After)
- **Aggregation (BFF)**: one round trip for a mobile home screen instead of six service calls
- **Transformation**: camelCase↔PascalCase, payload trimming for mobile, protocol translation (HTTP→gRPC to internal services)
- **Cross-cutting observability**: one place to log/trace every inbound request; correlation ids injected here
- **TLS termination, CORS, request size limits, WAF integration**

**What does NOT belong:**
- Business logic ('if the user is a gold member, also call X') — that's service/BFF orchestration creeping in; gateways rot into second application servers
- Database access, domain validation, workflow state
- Long-running request orchestration (gateway timeouts punish everyone)

**Deployment shapes:**
- Cloud-managed: Azure API Management, AWS API Gateway, Google Apigee — quotas, developer portals, policies out of the box
- Self-hosted proxies: Envoy, NGINX, Kong, YARP (.NET-native reverse proxy — popular for BFFs)
- One per client (BFF) vs one shared gateway — BFF multiplies deployment count but keeps client teams autonomous; mobile/web needs genuinely differ

**Failure modes to engineer for:**
- Gateway down = everything down — HA across zones, fast rolling deploys, health checks
- Gateway as bottleneck — stateless horizontal scaling, don't do heavy compute there
- Cascading aggregates — a BFF fan-out to 6 services multiplies partial-failure handling; timeouts must be tighter than client expectations
- Debugging indirection — distributed tracing (correlation ids through the gateway) is mandatory, not optional

data.title: Gateway responsibilities vs what stays in services
data.code:
Clients:  Web SPA    iOS app    Android app
              |          |           |
          Web BFF    Mobile BFF  Mobile BFF   (BFF per client)
              \          |          /
               API Gateway (auth, rate limit, routing, tracing)
              /     |        |       \
        Orders   Catalog  Payments  Identity   (own their data + AuthZ)

Web BFF aggregation example (home screen):
  GET /bff/home
    -> Orders.List(userId, 5)
    -> Recommendations.For(userId, 8)
    -> Notifications.UnreadCount(userId)
    merge -> { orders, recommendations, unreadCount }  // one client round trip

Rate limit policy at the edge:
  authenticated user: 600 req/min ; anonymous: 60/min
  exceeded -> 429 + Retry-After; mobile respects, web shows soft banner

Identity flow:
  gateway validates JWT signature/expiry ONCE
  forwards X-User-Id + claims to services
  services STILL enforce resource AuthZ (gateway can't know domain rules)

❌ Gateway anti-patterns:
  - 'gold members call Catalog AND Loyalty' written as gateway routing rules
  - gateway queries the Orders database directly
  - 30s aggregation with no per-upstream timeouts

data.title: Thin gateway, fat services
data.text: The graveyard of API gateways is full of business logic that crept in because 'it was easier at the edge'. Every domain rule in the gateway couples it to service internals and makes deploys a coordinated event. If logic is needed to compose responses, own it in an explicit BFF/orchestration layer you can test — and keep the gateway a policy-enforcing router.

items: Business logic accumulating in gateway policies — coordinated deployments return
No per-upstream timeouts on aggregates — one slow service holds every connection
Gateway doing heavy compute — it should route, not work
Treating gateway auth as full authorization — services must still check resource permissions
One shared gateway for clients with very different needs — mobile pays for web's aggregates
Deploying the gateway without tracing — debugging across the indirection becomes guesswork

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Gateway = single entry point: routing, authN, rate limits, transformation, tracing
BFF gives each client a gateway shaped to its needs and aggregates
Keep it thin: no business logic, no DB access, no long-running orchestration
It's the critical path: HA, fast deploys, per-upstream timeouts, mandatory tracing
data.takeaway: The gateway is where policy meets every request — put edge concerns there, keep domain logic out, and treat it with the availability discipline of a database.
